@sec-12-kernel-regression assembled the mechanics of reading a memory bank:
compare a query to stored keys, normalize the scores with row-wise softmax, and retrieve
a weighted blend of values. But its scoring rule was rigid. Euclidean distance treated all
coordinates equally, and validation tuned only a single scalar bandwidth $h$, which
scaled space uniformly, with no way to learn which features matter. With a fixed score,
only the input representation could adapt.

To break the sequence-to-sequence bottleneck of @sec-11-encoder-decoder, the
decoder must query the encoder's retained hidden states. In high dimensions, however,
fixed Euclidean distance is brittle. The decoder needs a similarity function that can
learn what constitutes a match for the task. This chapter gives the score its
own parameters.

Contrast this soft read with the hard lookup of an embedding table, which selects one row
by index. Selecting an encoder state by $\operatorname{argmax}$ would be piecewise constant
in the scores, leaving candidates that nearly matched with zero gradient. Instead, a
continuous softmax distribution over all keys lets the gradient of the training loss reach
the scoring parameters. Replacing fixed geometric distance with learned projections yields
**attention** (@fig-attention-lookup): a content-dependent, fully differentiable read whose
geometry adapts to the data.

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off - opening preview of the seeded date-rematch results. -->

The result is visible in the date task before we name all its parts. For the fixed
validation source

```text
may 17, 1971  ->  1971-05-17
```

the trained decoder emits the year first, even though those four characters reside at
the end of the source string. Across the fixed 400-example validation audit, the first
four attention rows place **97.5%** of their probability mass on the contextual encoder
states corresponding to the source-year characters. In the example above, emitting the
second character (`9`) allocates a maximum weight of 0.856 to the encoder state at the
source position of `9`, and emitting `7` assigns a peak weight of 0.985 to the encoder
state at the `7` in the year. These soft alignments emerge without explicit
supervision. The cross-entropy loss on the target characters alone determines where
the weights concentrate.

## The soft lookup and cross-attention {#the-scores-to-weights-machine-one-more-time}

Let the encoder retain its full memory

$$
\matr{H}=[\vect{h}_1,\ldots,\vect{h}_n]^\top
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_e}.
$$

At decoder step $t$, use the previous decoder hidden state
$\vect{s}_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_d}$ as the query. A learned compatibility function
$a_\theta$ produces one score per source position:

$$
e_{t,i}=a_\theta(\vect{s}_{t-1},\vect{h}_i).
$$

To exclude padding in variable-length sequences, let $M_i=0$ at valid source
positions and $M_i=-\infty$ at padded positions. Then

$$
\alpha_{t,i}
=\operatorname{softmax}_i(e_{t,i}+M_i),
\qquad
\vect{c}_t=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{t,i}\vect{h}_i.
$$ {#eq-learned-cross-attention}

This preserves the familiar $\matr{A}\matr{V}$ read of @sec-12-kernel-regression,
retaining the softmax normalization while replacing the rigid metric with a learned
scoring rule. Backpropagation can thus deliver gradients to the scoring parameters
through every valid memory slot. We have **softened the hard lookup**.

Because the query originates in the decoder while the memory resides in the encoder,
this operation is **cross-attention**: an interface bridging two distinct sequences.
The encoder's final state still initializes the decoder, but that initial handoff is no
longer the only path from source to output. By supplying every decoding step with its
own adaptive context vector $\vect{c}_t$, the architecture removes the **fixed-size state
bottleneck**. @sec-12-kernel-regression built the memory bank, and cross-attention now
learns the rule that reads it.

In @sec-08-cnn, stacked convolutions expanded receptive fields gradually through depth,
leaving a dense head to combine features across the image. By contrast, a single
cross-attention read scores every encoder position directly in one step, at the cost of
evaluating all query–key pairs. For now, however, the representations it queries still
originate from an RNN, which computes them sequentially, one step at a time.

## Additive attention: learn the comparison itself

The most direct way to make similarity learnable is to parameterize the compatibility
function with a shallow neural network. With the decoder query and the encoder key both
projected into a shared alignment space of width $d_a$, the additive score is

$$
e_{t,i}
=\vect{v}_a^\top
\tanh\!\left(
  \matr{W}_q\vect{s}_{t-1}
  +\matr{W}_k\vect{h}_i
\right),
$$ {#eq-additive-attention}

where

$$
\matr{W}_q\in\mathbb{R}^{d_a\times d_d},
\qquad
\matr{W}_k\in\mathbb{R}^{d_a\times d_e},
\qquad
\vect{v}_a\in\mathbb{R}^{d_a}.
$$

The two projections put vectors of different native widths, $d_d$ and $d_e$, into a
common alignment space. The $\tanh$ nonlinearity extracts joint match features, while
$\vect{v}_a$ weights their individual contributions to produce the scalar score. These
parameters are shared across all decoder steps and source positions: as the sliding
filter of @sec-08-cnn applied one learned template across an entire grid, attention
evaluates a single compatibility rule across all decoder–source pairs.

In batched execution, inserting a singleton sequence axis into the query tensor
$\matr{S}_{t-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times1\times d_d}$ allows it to broadcast across all
$n$ encoder positions in $\matr{H}$:

$$
\matr{S}_{t-1}\matr{W}_q^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B\times 1\times d_a},
\qquad
\matr{H}\matr{W}_k^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{B\times n\times d_a}.
$$

Passing their broadcast sum through $\tanh$ forms joint match features of shape
$(B,n,d_a)$, which $\vect{v}_a$ contracts into a $(B,n)$ score matrix. Normalizing
across the source axis via softmax produces a valid probability distribution over the
$n$ positions, and the resulting weighted read over $\matr{H}$ yields a $(B,d_e)$
context, one $d_e$-dimensional row for each sequence in the batch.

We fix one parameter setting to trace the arithmetic directly. With identity
projections and an all-ones selector, the scores of three source states evaluate to
$(1.015,1.562,1.124)$, which softmax converts into the weights
$(0.260,0.450,0.290)$:

```{python}
#| label: additive-scorer-snapshot
#| code-summary: "Code: compute the three-key additive scores and softmax weights"
#| code-fold: false
from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
torch.set_num_threads(4)  # pinned: results depend on the CPU thread count

# [1]
torch.manual_seed(6050)

query_snapshot = np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.2, -0.1])
key_snapshot = np.array([
    [-0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.0],
    [0.6, 0.5, 0.1, -0.2],
    [0.0, -0.4, 0.3, 0.2],
])
snapshot_scores = np.tanh(query_snapshot + key_snapshot).sum(axis=1)
snapshot_weights = np.exp(snapshot_scores - snapshot_scores.max())
snapshot_weights /= snapshot_weights.sum()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## "Learned kernel" is an analogy

Exponentiating a learned score and normalizing it reproduces the
Nadaraya--Watson algebra. Yet this does not make the scoring function a kernel in the
positive-semidefinite sense of kernel methods. Separate query and key projections leave
$a_\theta(\vect{q},\vect{k})$ neither symmetric nor positive semidefinite. What survives
is the operational pattern:
compare $\rightarrow$ normalize $\rightarrow$ mix.
:::

## Scaled dot product: from additive alignment to matrix products {#scaled-dot-product-learn-the-spaces-simplify-the-score}

Vectorizing additive attention over all $m$ decoder queries at once forms a
$(B,m,n,d_a)$ intermediate tensor, applies an elementwise tanh, and reduces it to
scalar scores. Scoring each query–key pair by its dot product avoids that intermediate
tensor and turns all comparisons into a single matrix multiplication. As in
@sec-01-linear-regression, where the dot product measured similarity against a
template, each key now acts as a template in a space learned during training.

To see how one query goes through the computation, compare a four-dimensional query
against three keys:

$$
\vect{q}=(0.9,\,-0.3,\,0.2,\,0.6),
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
\vect{k}_1&=(0.8,\,-0.2,\,0.1,\,0.5),\\
\vect{k}_2&=(-0.5,\,0.9,\,0.0,\,0.2),\\
\vect{k}_3&=(0.3,\,0.0,\,0.6,\,-0.4).
\end{aligned}
$$

Because $\vect{k}_1$ matches the sign pattern of $\vect{q}$ while $\vect{k}_2$ opposes its
largest coordinates, the raw dot products $\vect{q}^\top\vect{k}_j$ are
$(1.10,-0.60,0.15)$. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}=\sqrt{4}=2$ tempers these scores to
$(0.55,-0.30,0.075)$, and softmax converts them into the attention weights
$(0.488,0.209,0.303)$, placing nearly half the mass on the first key:

:::: {.plan-code}
::: {.plan}
1. Set a four-dimensional query and three keys, then compute `raw_walk`, `scaled_walk`,
   and `weight_walk`.
2. Run one query through dot product, scaling, and softmax.
:::

```{python}
#| label: scaled-dot-snapshot
#| code-summary: "Code: one query through dot product, scaling, and softmax"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
query_walk = torch.tensor([0.9, -0.3, 0.2, 0.6])
key_walk = torch.tensor([
    [0.8, -0.2, 0.1, 0.5],
    [-0.5, 0.9, 0.0, 0.2],
    [0.3, 0.0, 0.6, -0.4],
])
raw_walk = key_walk @ query_walk
scaled_walk = raw_walk / math.sqrt(query_walk.numel())
weight_walk = torch.softmax(scaled_walk, dim=0)
# [2]
print("raw scores:", raw_walk.numpy())
print("scaled scores:", scaled_walk.numpy())
print("weights:", weight_walk.numpy(), "sum:", weight_walk.sum().item())
```
::::
To run this comparison across an entire batch of sequences, project the decoder features
$\matr{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times m\times d_d}$ and encoder representations
$\matr{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times n\times d_e}$ into learned query, key, and value spaces:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\matr{Q}&=\matr{D}\matr{W}_Q\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times m\times d_k},
&\matr{W}_Q&\in\mathbb{R}^{d_d\times d_k},\\
\matr{K}&=\matr{H}\matr{W}_K\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times n\times d_k},
&\matr{W}_K&\in\mathbb{R}^{d_e\times d_k},\\
\matr{V}&=\matr{H}\matr{W}_V\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times n\times d_v},
&\matr{W}_V&\in\mathbb{R}^{d_e\times d_v}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The raw encoder and decoder widths $d_e$ and $d_d$ need not match: $\matr{W}_Q$ and
$\matr{W}_K$ map both into a shared comparison space of width $d_k$, while $\matr{W}_V$
projects values to an output width $d_v$. With an additive mask
$\matr{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times1\times n}$ broadcast across the $m$ queries to exclude
padded keys, **scaled dot-product attention** is

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(\matr{Q},\matr{K},\matr{V})
=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(
  \frac{\matr{Q}\matr{K}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}+\matr{M}
\right)\matr{V},
$$ {#eq-scaled-dot-product}

where $\matr{K}^{\top}$ transposes the last two axes of $\matr{K}$ to shape
$(B,d_k,n)$. The first matrix product $\matr{Q}\matr{K}^{\top}$ forms all $m\times n$
compatibility scores per batch item in a $(B,m,n)$ tensor. Applying softmax along the
last axis normalizes each query's scores over the $n$ keys into a weight matrix
$\matr{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times m\times n}$, and the second matrix product
$\matr{A}\matr{V}$ pools the values into an output of shape $(B,m,d_v)$. Whereas additive
attention forms a four-dimensional intermediate tensor, scaled dot-product attention
reduces the forward pass to two batched matrix multiplications ($\matr{Q}\matr{K}^{\top}$
and $\matr{A}\matr{V}$) that map directly onto optimized dense linear algebra
routines.^[@sec-a3-precision-performance turns that intuition into a conditional
performance model: dense products can reach high arithmetic intensity through reuse,
but shapes, data movement, implementation, and hardware determine the actual regime.]

Although a raw dot product is linear in each argument, the projections $\matr{W}_Q$ and
$\matr{W}_K$ learn which features and magnitudes to align on top of representations
that have already undergone nonlinear transformations.^[In @sec-14-self-attention-transformer,
a position-wise feedforward network will provide that nonlinear feature transformation
after recurrence disappears.]

### Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$?

Suppose, for the moment, that projected coordinates $q_\ell$ and $k_\ell$ are
independent and identically distributed with zero mean and unit variance, and that
their products are independent across coordinates. Then

$$
\E[\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k}]=0,
\qquad
\var(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})
=\sum_{\ell=1}^{d_k}\var(q_\ell k_\ell)=d_k.
$$

The score's standard deviation grows as $\sqrt{d_k}$, and dividing by that factor
returns the idealized variance to one. Geometrically, vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{d_k}$
with unit-variance coordinates concentrate near a thin spherical shell of radius
$\sqrt{d_k}$ ($\E[\norm{\vect{q}}^2]=\E[\norm{\vect{k}}^2]=d_k$). Although two
independent directions on that shell are nearly orthogonal, with typical $\cos\theta$
of order $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, multiplying both radii scales
$\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k}=\norm{\vect{q}}\,\norm{\vect{k}}\cos\theta$ to order $\sqrt{d_k}$.

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off - seeded sqrt(d_k) variance/softmax audit and results. -->

To illustrate how this growing spread concentrates the softmax weights, we draw
20,000 queries and 16 independent keys per query with standard normal coordinates at
widths $d_k\in\{8,32,128,512\}$. Each query's 16 raw scores are its dot products with
its keys. We compare the sample variance of the scores and the mean largest softmax
weight at each width, with and without division by $\sqrt{d_k}$:

:::: {.plan-code .plan-code-wide}
::: {.plan}
1. Create a seeded generator and an empty `scaling_rows` list for per-width results.
2. Audit score variance and softmax concentration versus width.
3. Print, for each width, the raw and scaled score variances and largest softmax
   weights.
:::

```{python}
#| label: sqrt-d-audit
#| code-summary: "Code: audit score variance and softmax concentration versus width"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
scaling_gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(6050132)
scaling_rows = []
# [2]
for width in (8, 32, 128, 512):
    raw_parts, raw_max_parts, scaled_max_parts = [], [], []
    for _ in range(20_000 // 500):
        q = torch.randn(500, 1, width, generator=scaling_gen)
        k = torch.randn(500, 16, width, generator=scaling_gen)
        raw = (q * k).sum(-1)
        raw_parts.append(raw.reshape(-1))
        raw_max_parts.append(torch.softmax(raw, dim=-1).max(-1).values)
        scaled_max_parts.append(
            torch.softmax(raw / math.sqrt(width), dim=-1).max(-1).values
        )
    raw_scores = torch.cat(raw_parts)
    scaling_rows.append((
        width,
        raw_scores.var(unbiased=True).item(),
        (raw_scores / math.sqrt(width)).var(unbiased=True).item(),
        torch.cat(raw_max_parts).mean().item(),
        torch.cat(scaled_max_parts).mean().item(),
    ))

# [3]
print("d_k   raw var   scaled var   raw max-w   scaled max-w")
for row in scaling_rows:
    print(f"{row[0]:3d}   {row[1]:8.3f}   {row[2]:10.3f}   "
          f"{row[3]:9.3f}   {row[4]:12.3f}")
```

```{python}
axes[1].plot(scaling_array[:, 0], scaling_array[:, 4], "s-",
             color="#232D4B", label="scaled")
axes[1].set(xscale="log", ylim=(0, 1), xlabel=r"projected width $d_k$",
            ylabel="mean largest weight", title="Control softmax concentration")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.show()
```
As $d_k$ increases from 8 to 512, raw variance rises from $8.02$ to $510.35$, whereas
scaled variance remains between $0.997$ and $1.004$. Over the same range, the mean
largest unscaled softmax weight climbs from $0.564$ to $0.944$, while the scaled value
stays between $0.24$ and $0.25$, well above the uniform baseline of $1/16=0.0625$
and far below one-hot saturation at $1.0$. This is the **temperature dial** of
@sec-02-logistic-softmax, set by the dimension. Scaling corrects the
dimension-induced spread without normalizing the vectors, and trained projections need
not remain independent or keep unit variance.

<!-- /NOVEL -->

## Excluding padded positions before softmax {#mask-before-softmax-and-mask-the-right-thing}

Padding affects two computations, as @sec-11-encoder-decoder showed: the loss and an
encoder's final state. Attention introduces a third site where sequence lengths must be
enforced: the score matrix. A padded key must not merely receive a low score. It must be
excluded from normalization entirely. Setting its score to zero fails because
$\exp(0)=1$ still contributes a positive term to the normalizing sum. Instead, scores at
padded positions must be set to $-\infty$ before softmax so that $\exp(-\infty)=0$.

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off - independent mask implementation and all-masked guard. -->

The scaled-dot operator below accepts already projected
queries, keys, and values, then audits a batch whose second example has two padded
keys:

:::: {.plan-code .plan-code-wide}
::: {.plan}
1. Define the reusable `scaled_dot_attention` helper.
2. Run and audit scaled dot-product attention with a source-padding mask.
:::

```{python}
#| label: padding-mask-audit
#| code-summary: "Code: scaled dot-product attention with a source-padding mask"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
def scaled_dot_attention(
    queries: torch.Tensor,
    keys: torch.Tensor,
    values: torch.Tensor,
    key_is_valid: torch.Tensor,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    """Attend with Q:(B,m,d_k), K:(B,n,d_k), V:(B,n,d_v)."""
    if queries.ndim != 3 or keys.ndim != 3 or values.ndim != 3:
        raise ValueError("Q, K, and V must be three-dimensional")
    if queries.shape[-1] != keys.shape[-1]:
        raise ValueError("projected Q and K widths must match")
    if keys.shape[:2] != values.shape[:2]:
        raise ValueError("K and V must have the same batch and key axes")
    if key_is_valid.shape != keys.shape[:2] or not key_is_valid.any(dim=1).all():
        raise ValueError("every example needs at least one valid key")

    scores = queries @ keys.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(keys.shape[-1])
    scores = scores.masked_fill(~key_is_valid[:, None, :], -torch.inf)
    weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return weights @ values, weights

# [2]
mask_gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(6050133)
Q_demo = torch.randn(2, 2, 4, generator=mask_gen)
K_demo = torch.randn(2, 4, 4, generator=mask_gen)
V_demo = torch.randn(2, 4, 3, generator=mask_gen)
valid_demo = torch.tensor([[True, True, True, True],
                           [True, True, False, False]])
context_demo, mask_weights = scaled_dot_attention(
    Q_demo, K_demo, V_demo, valid_demo
)
assert torch.allclose(
    mask_weights.sum(-1), torch.ones_like(mask_weights[..., 0])
)
assert torch.count_nonzero(mask_weights[1, :, 2:]) == 0
print("Q", tuple(Q_demo.shape), "K", tuple(K_demo.shape),
      "V", tuple(V_demo.shape), "A", tuple(mask_weights.shape),
      "AV", tuple(context_demo.shape))
print("maximum row-sum error:",
      f"{(mask_weights.sum(-1) - 1).abs().max().item():.2e}")
print("maximum padded weight:",
      f"{mask_weights[1, :, 2:].max().item():.1f}")
```
::::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-padding-mask
#| fig-alt: "A two-row by four-column attention heatmap contains numeric weights in the first two key columns. The final two columns are labeled PAD in both rows and have zero weight."
#| fig-cap: "A source-padding mask acts before softmax. The second example has only two real keys, so its last two score cells are excluded and receive exactly zero weight. Cross-attention may read every real source position, so no causal triangle belongs here."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 2.5), constrained_layout=True)
shown = mask_weights[1].detach().numpy()
image = ax.imshow(shown, vmin=0, vmax=shown.max(), cmap="magma", aspect="auto")
for row in range(shown.shape[0]):
    for col in range(shown.shape[1]):
        label = "PAD" if col >= 2 else f"{shown[row, col]:.2f}"
        ax.text(col, row, label, ha="center", va="center",
                color="white" if shown[row, col] < 0.65 * shown.max() else "black")
ax.set(xticks=range(4), xticklabels=["key 1", "key 2", "pad", "pad"],
       yticks=range(2), yticklabels=["query 1", "query 2"],
       xlabel="source/key position", title="Mask source padding before softmax")

plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Trap: conflating the three sequence masks

The target loss mask specifies which output positions should not be graded. It is
included for generality, although all ISO targets here share the same length. The
cross-attention padding mask specifies which source positions do not exist. A causal mask
prevents positions from attending to future tokens. Because our recurrent decoder
generates one step at a time and the full source is already available, only the
source-padding mask is needed here. @sec-14-self-attention-transformer will
introduce causal masking inside decoder self-attention.

An all-masked row has no valid probability distribution and makes softmax over all
$-\infty$ undefined (`NaN`). An implementation should assert that every example
contains at least one real key, as the function above does.
:::

We rerun the date task, altering a single architectural component while holding these
settings fixed:

- the same date generator and duplicate-source rejection;
- the same train/validation/test split;
- the same embedding width 32 and LSTM hidden width 128;
- the same optimizer, learning rate, batch size, 25 epochs, teacher forcing, gradient
  clipping, and seed;
- the same first 400 unambiguous validation sources for every learning curve;
- one final exact-match evaluation on the same 437 unambiguous test sources.

Below, we copy the generator and split of @sec-11-encoder-decoder byte for byte,
ensuring both models train on identical examples:

```{python}
#| label: date-data-rematch
#| code-summary: "Code: reconstruct Chapter 13's sealed date benchmark"
#| code-fold: false
import random, torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# [1]
MONTHS = ["january", "february", "march", "april", "may", "june", "july",
          "august", "september", "october", "november", "december"]
DAYS = dict(zip(MONTHS, [31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31]))

# [2]
def make_date(rng: random.Random) -> tuple[str, str]:
    mo = rng.randrange(12)
    d = rng.randrange(1, DAYS[MONTHS[mo]] + 1)
    y = rng.randrange(1950, 2026)
    iso = f"{y:04d}-{mo+1:02d}-{d:02d}"
    style = rng.random()
    if style < 0.35:
        src = f"{MONTHS[mo]} {d}, {y}"
    elif style < 0.6:
        src = f"{d} {MONTHS[mo]} {y}"
    elif rng.random() < 0.7:
        src = f"{mo+1:02d}/{d:02d}/{y}"            # US convention: mm/dd
    else:
        src = f"{d:02d}/{mo+1:02d}/{y}"            # EU convention: dd/mm
    return src, iso

rng = random.Random(6050)
pairs, seen_sources = [], set()
# [3]
while len(pairs) < 9000:
    pair = make_date(rng)
    if pair[0] not in seen_sources:
        seen_sources.add(pair[0])
        pairs.append(pair)
train_pairs = pairs[:8000]
valid_pairs = pairs[8000:8500]
test_pairs = pairs[8500:]
# [4]
print(*pairs[:4], sep="\n")
train_sources = {s for s, _ in train_pairs}
valid_sources = {s for s, _ in valid_pairs}
test_sources = {s for s, _ in test_pairs}
print("exact-source overlaps: "
      f"train/valid {len(train_sources & valid_sources)}, "
      f"train/test {len(train_sources & test_sources)}, "
      f"valid/test {len(valid_sources & test_sources)}")

PAD, BOS, EOS = 0, 1, 2                             # special tokens first
SRC = sorted(set("".join(s for s, _ in pairs)))
TGT = sorted(set("".join(t for _, t in pairs)))
src_stoi = {c: i + 3 for i, c in enumerate(SRC)}
tgt_stoi = {c: i + 3 for i, c in enumerate(TGT)}
tgt_itos = {i: c for c, i in tgt_stoi.items()}
V_src, V_tgt = len(SRC) + 3, len(TGT) + 3
print(f"source vocab {V_src}, target vocab {V_tgt}")
```
::::
Because numeric dates can be ambiguous, we retain the unambiguous subsets defined
in @sec-11-encoder-decoder. Heatmap inspections, like design decisions, use the
validation split alone.

### Put the learned read inside the recurrent decoder

The packed encoder now returns three outputs: its final $(\vect{h},\vect{c})$ state,
which still initializes the decoder; a padded memory tensor containing all
real encoder representations; and a validity mask excluding padded slots. At step $t$:

1. use the previous decoder hidden state $\vect{s}_{t-1}$ as the query;
2. compute additive scores over the encoder memory and mask padding;
3. form the context vector $\vect{c}_t$;
4. concatenate $\vect{c}_t$ with the embedding of the previous target token;
5. advance the decoder LSTM by one step, then predict from
   $[\vect{s}_t;\vect{c}_t]$.

This timing follows the [Bahdanau](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473)-style formulation.
Luong-style variants often score with the current decoder state instead. Both are valid,
but silently mixing their indexing obscures which decoder state supplied the query for
each context vector.

For this date model, every tensor shape is concrete:

| quantity | shape |
|---|---|
| previous hidden query | $(B,128)$ |
| encoder memory | $(B,T_{\text{src}},128)$ |
| attention weights | $(B,T_{\text{src}})$ |
| context | $(B,128)$ |
| token embedding joined with context | $(B,1,160)$ |
| decoder output | $(B,1,128)$ |
| output-head input $[\vect{s}_t;\vect{c}_t]$ | $(B,256)$ |

<!-- NOVEL: needs sign-off - independently written attentive date model and rematch. -->

:::: {.plan-code .plan-code-wide}
::: {.plan}
1. Define the reusable helpers: `batchify`, `unambiguous`, and `LearnedAlignment`.
2. Filter validation and test pairs with `unambiguous`, and keep the first 400
   validation pairs as a fixed set.
3. Run a masked additive-attention LSTM decoder.
4. Define the reusable helpers: `AttentiveSeq2Seq`, `greedy_batch`, and `exact_match`.
:::

```{python}
#| label: attentive-seq2seq
#| code-summary: "Code: a masked additive-attention LSTM decoder"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
def batchify(prs: list[tuple[str, str]], idx: list[int]) -> tuple[
    torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor
]:
    srcs = [torch.tensor([src_stoi[c] for c in prs[i][0]]) for i in idx]
    lengths = torch.tensor([len(s) for s in srcs])
    tgts = [torch.tensor([BOS] + [tgt_stoi[c] for c in prs[i][1]] + [EOS])
            for i in idx]
    S = nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(srcs, batch_first=True, padding_value=PAD)
    T = nn.utils.rnn.pad_sequence(tgts, batch_first=True, padding_value=PAD)
    return S, lengths, T

def unambiguous(prs: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    return [(s, t) for s, t in prs
            if "/" not in s or int(s[:2]) > 12 or int(s[3:5]) > 12]

# [2]
valid_unamb = unambiguous(valid_pairs)
test_unamb = unambiguous(test_pairs)
valid_fixed = valid_unamb[:400]
# [3]
print(f"fixed validation {len(valid_fixed)}; final test {len(test_unamb)}")

class LearnedAlignment(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden: int = 128, alignment: int = 128):
        super().__init__()
        self.key_map = nn.Linear(hidden, alignment, bias=False)
        self.query_map = nn.Linear(hidden, alignment, bias=False)
        self.selector = nn.Linear(alignment, 1, bias=False)

    def forward(
        self,
        memory: torch.Tensor,
        query: torch.Tensor,
        valid: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        match_features = torch.tanh(
            self.key_map(memory) + self.query_map(query).unsqueeze(1)
        )                                                   # (B, T_src, d_a)
        scores = self.selector(match_features).squeeze(-1)  # (B, T_src)
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~valid, -torch.inf)
        weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
        context = torch.bmm(weights.unsqueeze(1), memory).squeeze(1)
        return context, weights

# [4]
class AttentiveSeq2Seq(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, v_src: int, v_tgt: int, embed: int = 32,
                 hidden: int = 128, alignment: int = 128):
        super().__init__()
        self.src_emb = nn.Embedding(v_src, embed, padding_idx=PAD)
        self.tgt_emb = nn.Embedding(v_tgt, embed, padding_idx=PAD)
        self.encoder = nn.LSTM(embed, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.attention = LearnedAlignment(hidden, alignment)
        self.decoder = nn.LSTM(embed + hidden, hidden, batch_first=True)
        self.out = nn.Linear(2 * hidden, v_tgt)

    def encode(
        self, S: torch.Tensor, lengths: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]:
        packed = nn.utils.rnn.pack_padded_sequence(
            self.src_emb(S), lengths, batch_first=True, enforce_sorted=False)
        packed_memory, state = self.encoder(packed)
        memory, _ = nn.utils.rnn.pad_packed_sequence(
            packed_memory, batch_first=True, total_length=S.shape[1])
        valid = torch.arange(S.shape[1])[None, :] < lengths[:, None]
        return memory, state, valid

    def decode_step(
        self,
        token: torch.Tensor,
        state: tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor],
        memory: torch.Tensor,
        valid: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]:
        query = state[0][-1]                              # previous hidden state
        context, weights = self.attention(memory, query, valid)
        decoder_input = torch.cat(
            (self.tgt_emb(token), context.unsqueeze(1)), dim=-1
        )
        decoder_output, state = self.decoder(decoder_input, state)
        logits = self.out(torch.cat((decoder_output[:, 0], context), dim=-1))
        return logits, state, weights

    def forward(
        self, S: torch.Tensor, lengths: torch.Tensor, T_in: torch.Tensor,
    ) -> torch.Tensor:
        memory, state, valid = self.encode(S, lengths)
        logits = []
        for t in range(T_in.shape[1]):
            logit, state, _ = self.decode_step(
                T_in[:, t:t + 1], state, memory, valid)
            logits.append(logit)
        return torch.stack(logits, dim=1)                 # (B, T_tgt, V_tgt)

@torch.inference_mode()
def greedy_batch(
    model: AttentiveSeq2Seq,
    prs: list[tuple[str, str]],
    batch: int = 128,
    maxlen: int = 12,
) -> list[tuple[str, str, torch.Tensor]]:
    model.eval()
    outputs = []
    for start in range(0, len(prs), batch):
        subset = prs[start:start + batch]
        S, lengths, _ = batchify(subset, list(range(len(subset))))
        memory, state, valid = model.encode(S, lengths)
        token = torch.full((len(subset), 1), BOS)
        token_steps, weight_steps = [], []
        for _ in range(maxlen):
            logits, state, weights = model.decode_step(
                token, state, memory, valid)
            token = logits.argmax(-1, keepdim=True)
            token_steps.append(token[:, 0])
            weight_steps.append(weights)
        predicted = torch.stack(token_steps, dim=1)
        attention = torch.stack(weight_steps, dim=1)
        for row, (source, _) in enumerate(subset):
            chars = []
            for index in predicted[row].tolist():
                if index == EOS:
                    break
                chars.append(tgt_itos.get(index, "?"))
            outputs.append((
                source,
                "".join(chars),
                attention[row, :, :lengths[row]].clone(),
            ))
    return outputs

@torch.inference_mode()
def exact_match(
    model: AttentiveSeq2Seq, prs: list[tuple[str, str]],
) -> float:
    generated = greedy_batch(model, prs)
    return sum(
        guess == truth
        for (_, truth), (_, guess, _) in zip(prs, generated)
    ) / len(prs)
```
::::
Several elements change relative to @sec-11-encoder-decoder. The embeddings and
encoder width remain untouched. Values are now the contextual encoder states themselves,
while learned linear projections construct match features for keys and queries.
The decoder must now advance one step at a time because each subsequent context
depends on the preceding decoder state. Teacher forcing still supplies the true previous
token, but it no longer permits a single fused RNN call over the target sequence.

### Attention on the matched schedule {#the-matched-schedule-rematch}

The fixed-state baseline curve is the validation trajectory recorded for the packed,
teacher-forced model in @sec-11-encoder-decoder (@fig-tf-vs-fr). We reuse those
recorded values, train the attentive model once, and inspect its validation alignments,
and we evaluate on the test split once, after the model is fixed:

:::: {.plan-code .plan-code-wide}
::: {.plan}
1. Set the checkpoint epochs and @sec-11-encoder-decoder's frozen curve, then build
   `AttentiveSeq2Seq` and its optimizer.
2. Matched-schedule date rematch and reused-endpoint audit.
3. Print both validation curves, parameter counts, one decoded example, alignment
   audits, and the test result.
:::

```{python}
#| label: attention-date-training
#| code-summary: "Code: matched-schedule date rematch and reused-endpoint audit"
#| code-fold: false
# [1]
checkpoints = (2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 25)
baseline_curve = {
    2: 0.0025, 4: 0.1475, 6: 0.5375, 8: 0.7575,
    12: 0.9500, 16: 0.9500, 20: 0.9950, 25: 0.9575,
}

torch.manual_seed(6050)
attention_model = AttentiveSeq2Seq(V_src, V_tgt)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(attention_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
attention_curve = {}

# [2]
for epoch in range(1, 26):
    attention_model.train()
    permutation = torch.randperm(len(train_pairs))
    for start in range(0, len(train_pairs), 128):
        ids = permutation[start:start + 128].tolist()
        S, lengths, T = batchify(train_pairs, ids)
        logits = attention_model(S, lengths, T[:, :-1])
        loss = F.cross_entropy(
            logits.reshape(-1, V_tgt),
            T[:, 1:].reshape(-1),
            ignore_index=PAD,
        )
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(attention_model.parameters(), 5.0)
        optimizer.step()
    if epoch in checkpoints:
        attention_curve[epoch] = exact_match(
            attention_model, valid_fixed)

# [3]
print("epoch   fixed-state   attention")
for epoch in checkpoints:
    print(f"{epoch:2d}       {baseline_curve[epoch]:6.2%}       "
          f"{attention_curve[epoch]:6.2%}")

validation_outputs = greedy_batch(attention_model, valid_fixed)
source_example, truth_example = valid_fixed[0]           # fixed before training
_, generated_example, alignment_example = validation_outputs[0]

year_mass, year_top1, row_errors = [], [], []
for (source, _), (_, _, weights) in zip(valid_fixed, validation_outputs):
    year_positions = list(range(len(source) - 4, len(source)))
    for step in range(4):
        year_mass.append(weights[step, year_positions].sum().item())
        year_top1.append(int(weights[step].argmax().item() in year_positions))
    row_errors.append((weights[:10].sum(1) - 1).abs().max().item())

attention_params = sum(p.numel() for p in attention_model.parameters())
baseline_params = 169_326
print(f"parameters: baseline {baseline_params:,}; "
      f"attention {attention_params:,} "
      f"(+{(attention_params / baseline_params - 1):.1%})")
print(f"validation example: {source_example!r} -> "
      f"{generated_example!r} (truth {truth_example})")
print(f"validation year-region mass: {np.mean(year_mass):.3%}; "
      f"top key in region: {np.mean(year_top1):.3%}")
print("maximum validation row-sum error:", f"{max(row_errors):.2e}")

test_exact = exact_match(attention_model, test_unamb)     # one final test audit
print(f"one final test audit ({len(test_unamb)} sources): "
      f"baseline 93.1%; attention {test_exact:.1%}")
```

At epoch 6, the fixed-state baseline reaches $53.75\%$ while the attentive model attains

::: {.callout-warning}
## Trap: confounding bottleneck removal with model capacity

Although we matched the dataset, hidden dimensions, optimizer, initial seed, and epoch
budget, this comparison is **not** a single-variable ablation. The attentive model
has 269,550 parameters compared to the baseline's 169,326 (a 59.2% increase), and its
per-step attention mechanism incurs more FLOPs. Initializing these additional
projection layers also consumes pseudo-random draws before the first shuffle, subtly
altering minibatch ordering. Faster convergence across epochs shows an empirical
advantage of the attentive architecture in this single seeded run, but it does not
isolate bottleneck removal from added model capacity as the sole underlying cause.
:::

The heatmap addresses a more specific question. On the fixed validation example, the
year must travel from the last four source positions to the first four outputs. The
boxed region catches that movement, and across all 400 fixed validation examples, the
first four attention rows place 97.5% of their probability mass on the contextual
encoder states corresponding to the source-year characters. The top-weighted state
falls within that region 99.7% of the time.

::: {.callout-note title="Reading the heatmap"}
Columns are indexed by source characters, but their values are contextual hidden states.
Because each state summarizes a recurrent prefix, the representation at a delimiter can
readily encode information about preceding tokens. Attention weights reflect internal
computational routing, not calibrated predictive confidence or a causal explanation of
the model.
:::

<!-- /NOVEL -->

## One head in the date model {#one-learned-view-for-now}

The date model uses a single learned additive scorer and one weighted context vector.
Its query and key projections compute alignment scores, while the encoder states supply
retrieval values. Multi-head routing, in which parallel projections allow distinct
heads to attend to multiple features simultaneously, is developed
in @sec-14-self-attention-transformer.

## Recurrence remains: the serial bottleneck {#the-bottleneck-that-remains}

Cross-attention resolves the fixed-state bottleneck of sequence-to-sequence models:
every decoder output can read any encoder state through a learned, differentiable soft
address. For the year field of the date task, the learned weights concentrate on the
encoder states indexed by the source-year characters, without explicit alignment
supervision.

Yet the host networks are still recurrent: $\vect{h}_i$ depends on $\vect{h}_{i-1}$,
and $\vect{s}_t$ depends on $\vect{s}_{t-1}$. Because the hidden states of a sequence
cannot be computed in parallel during training, the number of sequential steps grows
with sequence length. This constraint motivates the next architectural transition:
can self-attention replace recurrence entirely by allowing every token to attend across
its own sequence in parallel? @sec-14-self-attention-transformer answers that question.

::: {.callout-note}
## Check yourself

Close the book for one minute and reconstruct the soft lookup.

- What distinct jobs do queries, keys, and values perform?
- Why does masking belong inside score normalization?
- What does a learnable compatibility function gain over a fixed kernel?
:::

## Okay, so: attention softens the address

1. **Attention softens the address.** @sec-11-encoder-decoder learned embedding
   representations while keeping lookup indices hard. The softmax of
   @sec-02-logistic-softmax makes the lookup differentiable: learned scores become a
   probability distribution over memory locations.
2. **Additive attention learns the compatibility function.** Query and key are
   projected into a shared alignment space, a $\tanh$ nonlinearity creates match
   features, and a linear selector produces each scalar score. The same scorer is
   reused across all decoder–source pairs.
3. **Cross-attention bridges two sequences.** Queries originate in the decoder while
   keys and values reside in the encoder. Each step forms its own context vector, so the
   final state of @sec-11-encoder-decoder is no longer the only path from source to
   output.
4. **Scaled dot product learns comparison spaces.** Projected
   $\matr{Q}\matr{K}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k}$ maps directly to dense matrix products.
   Under the idealized independent unit-variance model, scaling holds score variance
   near one instead of letting it grow with $d_k$.
5. **Masking is part of the operator.** Padding must be excluded before softmax.
   Setting a padded score to zero fails to mask it. Cross-attention attends over all
   valid source positions, while causal masking belongs to the self-attentive
   decoder in @sec-14-self-attention-transformer.
6. **On dates, attention learns where to read.** Under the shared schedule, attention
   reaches 93.25% validation exact match at epoch 6 and 100.0% on the final test
   audit. Across the validation set, the four rows that emit the year allocate 97.5% of
   their weight to states indexed by the source-year region. Parameter count and
   compute were not matched: the attentive model has 59.2% more parameters.

The recurrent networks that construct this memory bank remain in place for now.
@sec-14-self-attention-transformer lets a sequence query itself, routing context across
positions so that recurrence becomes optional.

## Sources and further reading {.unnumbered}

- [Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio, *Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473): conjectures that the fixed-length encoder vector is a bottleneck, then tests differentiable soft search with an additive scorer.
- [Luong, Pham, and Manning, *Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation*](https://aclanthology.org/D15-1166/): compares dot, general, and concat scoring functions and clarifies a second recurrent-attention timing convention.
- [Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/7181-attention-is-all-you-need): introduces scaled dot-product and multi-head attention in the Transformer architecture that @sec-14-self-attention-transformer develops.
